explanations: luna: The section's root gloss for ء م ن treats believing as affirming a true word; these people say they believe in God and the Last Day, while the verse says they are not believers, a direct boundary between speech and inward truth. | terra: People say they believe in God and the Last Day although they are not believers, exposing a profession whose state contradicts its wording.

luna: The section says a word may lie in speech and deed; these speakers claim faith while trying to deceive God and believers, though the verse says they deceive only themselves, completing the false profession in 2:8.

luna: The section locates trust in the heart's stillness; this continuation describes disease in the hearts of those who falsely profess belief, making their inward disorder the opposite of that stillness. | terra: Disease in their hearts grows and punishment follows because they lie; this supplies the inward condition behind the false profession of 2:8.
terra: Those in doubt about the revealed word are challenged to produce a comparable surah and call their witnesses if they are truthful, turning suspicion into a public truth test.
luna: The verse forbids mixing truth with falsehood or knowingly concealing truth; it states the boundary between genuine testimony and the fabricated or misleading speech developed in the section.
terra: Some People of the Book wish to turn believers back into unbelief after faith; ردد becomes reversal from accepted truth to rejected truth.
terra: Exclusive claims to Paradise are met with “Bring your proof, if you are truthful,” requiring a claimed religious word to bear evidence.

luna: The section treats al-balad al-amīn as a secure city; this verse says God made the House a place people return to and a security, giving the sanctuary at Mecca the same protective function. | terra: God makes the House a place repeatedly returned to and a security (أَمْنًا), combining dependable return, staying, and sanctuary around the place sworn by in 95:3.

luna: Ibrahim asks God to make this place بَلَدًا آمِنًا and provide its people; the verse gives the secure city named in 95:3 a concrete prayer and provision context. | terra: Abraham asks God to make “this a secure city” (بَلَدًا ءَامِنًا), the closest syntactic and spatial counterpart to “this secure city” in 95:3.

luna: The section's 95:6 joins belief with righteous action; this account of righteousness includes belief and fulfilling a promise when made, making reliable action part of what genuine faith looks like.
terra: A person’s speech about worldly life impresses and he calls God to witness his heart, while he is actually the fiercest opponent; 2:205 exposes the deed behind the display.
terra: Once the impressive speaker turns away, he destroys crops and offspring; this ayah supplies the action that falsifies the words described in 2:204.
terra: The Ark is given as a sign of kingship and contains tranquility from the Lord; an entrusted sign makes reassurance tangible.
terra: Rejecting false authority and believing in God is grasping a firm handhold that never breaks, rendering stable faith as physical attachment.

luna: Ibrahim says he believes but asks to see the raising of birds “so my heart may be at rest”; the verse makes faith and settled assurance coexist, as the section's account of iman and security does. | terra: Abraham already believes, yet asks to see resurrection “so that my heart may be reassured”; faith and the heart’s further settling are distinguished without being opposed.

terra: The debt ayah regulates writing and witness so a disputed obligation can be trusted; this legal setting concretely approaches the section’s dictionary sense of crediting a person in adjudication.

luna: The section defines amānah against betrayal; in its debt instructions this verse says that when people trust one another, the entrusted person must discharge the trust and fear God. | terra: When one person trusts another, the entrusted person must discharge the trust (أَمَٰنَتَهُ); the ayah states interpersonal confidence and its opposite, betrayal, in the section’s own root.
terra: Firm verses are the Book’s foundation, while deviant hearts chase ambiguity; those rooted in knowledge answer “We believe in it,” joining firm word and stable reception.
terra: After the rooted believers’ confession in 3:7, they ask God not to let their hearts deviate after guidance, naming stability as a continuing gift.
terra: The prayer affirms that God will gather humanity for an undoubted Day because God does not fail the appointment, directly linking Judgment to a reliable promise.
luna: This repeats the command not to mix truth with falsehood or conceal it knowingly, showing the same specific boundary in an address to the People of the Book.

luna: This verse describes people twisting their tongues so listeners think a statement belongs to Scripture when it does not, and attributing it to God; it is a specific word-made falsehood of the kind the section contrasts with true revelation.
terra: The people described disbelieve after belief despite testifying that the Messenger is true, making rejected testimony a reversal of prior assent.

luna: The sanctuary is a clear sign and whoever enters it is safe (آمِنًا); this ties the section's secure-city image to the Kaaba and its protected entry. | terra: Whoever enters the House is safe, giving the secure-place image of 95:3 a concrete sanctuary rule.
terra: Obeying a faction of the People of the Book would turn believers back to unbelief, warning that the wrong trusted speakers can reverse assent.
terra: Divine help is made good news so believers’ hearts may be reassured by it; the promised sign serves inward rest.
terra: Obeying unbelievers would turn the believers back on their heels, turning trust in hostile counsel into loss.
terra: The hypocrites say with their mouths what is absent from their hearts, locating the instability of speech in a divided interior.
terra: A frightening human report increases the believers’ faith, and they answer that God is sufficient and the best trustee; trusted reliance settles rather than amplifies the threat.

luna: The section defines amānah as the opposite of betrayal and ends with God as الحكم; this verse commands that trusts be returned to their owners and that people be judged justly, joining those two claims in one command from God. | terra: God commands trusts to be returned to their owners and judgments to be made justly, joining amānah to the judging function of 95:8.
terra: Believers who dispute are commanded to refer the matter back (فَرُدُّوهُ) to God and the Messenger, turning “return” into trust in the authoritative word.

luna: The verse describes people who claim belief in revelation but seek judgment from false authorities after being told to reject them; this is a specific refusal to trust the revealed judge. | terra: People claim belief in revelation while seeking judgment from false authority, making their chosen judge contradict their spoken īmān.

luna: When called to Allah and the Messenger, the hypocrites turn away; this verse gives the same refusal of a trusted judgment that 4:60 introduces. | terra: When told to come to God’s revelation and the Messenger, the hypocrites turn away; their act verifies the false claim exposed in 4:60.

luna: The section's dictionary gloss for د ي ن includes trusting someone in judgment, while its gloss for ء م ن makes faith assent; here true belief requires making the Messenger judge and inwardly accepting his ruling without resistance. | terra: Faith is denied until the hearers accept the Prophet as judge, find no inward unease at his decision, and submit fully; belief, accepted judgment, and inward rest are one sequence.
luna: The section says a lie can occur in word and act; these people say “obedience” to the Messenger, then privately plan otherwise, a direct case of speech contradicted by deed.
terra: Reports of security or fear should be referred back to the Messenger and competent authorities, linking reliable news, proper return, and the two states defining amn.
terra: The certain gathering for Resurrection is sealed by “Who is truer than God in statement?”, joining Judgment to the Speaker’s unsurpassable truthfulness.
luna: The section glosses al-Muʾmin as the One who fulfills His promise; this verse says Satan promises people but gives them only delusion, a direct contrary promise.
terra: After promising believers lasting gardens, the ayah asks, “Who is truer than God in speech?” directly grounds faith in the reliability of His promise.

luna: This command requires believers to stand firmly for justice as witnesses even against themselves or relatives; it is a specific scene of truthful testimony under judgment that fits the section's trust-and-verdict link.
terra: People believe, disbelieve, believe again, and then deepen in disbelief; the repeated reversals enact an unrooted heart’s movement between assent and denial.
terra: The hypocrites are “wavering between” two sides and belong fully to neither, a nonlexical portrait of the unsettled heart.

luna: The section distinguishes accepting truth from merely saying words; this verse describes people whose mouths say “we believe” while their hearts do not, and who listen eagerly to lies, joining false profession to false report. | terra: Some say “we believe” with their mouths while their hearts do not believe, and they distort words, combining false profession with corrupted transmission.
terra: The judgment of ignorance is set against the question, “Who is better than God in judgment for people who are certain?”, a close counterpart to 95:8’s final appeal.
terra: When the listeners hear revelation, they recognize its truth and openly affirm belief, showing trustworthy speech arriving at sincere assent.
luna: God says He made the Kaaba, the Sacred House, a standing support for people; this gives the “secure city” image a concrete sanctuary at its center.

luna: The disciples ask Jesus for a table from heaven so their hearts may be reassured; the verse gives a concrete case where faith and a request for inward certainty meet. | terra: The disciples want the table so that “our hearts may be reassured” and so they may know that Jesus has spoken truth; trusted speech and a settled heart meet explicitly.

luna: The same paired charge—fabricating about God or denying His signs—appears here, with the verse adding that such wrongdoers do not succeed; it makes the section's true-making/false-making contrast consequential.
terra: Before the Fire the deniers say that, if returned, they would no longer deny the signs and would become believers; the row contributes their professed change of trust.
terra: God says that if they were returned they would return to what was forbidden and that they are liars, joining both kinds of “return” to the exposure of a false promise in 6:27.
terra: God distinguishes calling the Prophet a liar from rejecting God’s signs: “they do not call you false” (لَا يُكَذِّبُونَكَ), directly illuminating the alternate personal object in 95:7.
terra: Earlier messengers endured being denied until God’s help came, and none can change God’s words; rejection by hearers cannot falsify the promise.

luna: This verse says judgment belongs to God, who relates the truth and is the best of deciders; it brings the section's final claim about God's judgment into an explicit dispute over the warning. | terra: The Prophet says judgment belongs only to God and that He relates the truth, joining true declaration to the decisive Judge.

luna: After death, people are returned to God, their true Master, for judgment; the section's root gloss for ر د د includes returning and its dīn gloss concerns trust in judgment, which this verse brings together.
terra: Being turned back after guidance is pictured as a bewildered person wandering while companions call him to guidance, directly enacting the section’s lost, back-and-forth sense of ردد.
terra: Abraham asks which of the two parties has the stronger right to security, after contrasting his lack of fear with his people’s fear; 6:82 gives the verdict for uncorrupted faith.

luna: The section links the ء م ن root in faith with the removal of fear; this verse promises security to those who believe and do not mix their faith with wrongdoing, an explicit Quranic joining of iman and safety. | terra: Those who believe without clothing their faith in wrongdoing are the ones to whom security belongs, placing the two branches of ء م ن in one sentence.
luna: The claim that God revealed nothing to a human is answered by recalling the scripture given to Moses; the verse sets denial of revelation against a named, actual act of divine sending.

luna: This verse calls it a grave wrong to claim revelation falsely or to say “I will reveal like what God revealed”; it gives a concrete case of a human counterfeiting God's creative authority. | terra: Inventing a lie against God includes falsely claiming revelation or claiming the ability to reveal like God; the death scene then exposes the pretended speaker.

luna: The section's dictionary example for ك ذ ب is cloth ornamented to look different from its true state; this verse says devils inspire one another with embellished speech as deception, a direct verbal counterpart to that deceptive surface.

luna: This continuation says that hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter incline to the deceptive speech and become pleased with it; it shows a heart settling on falsehood rather than the section's secure truth.

luna: The section ends by calling God the supreme judge and distinguishes genuine revelation from invention; this verse asks whether one should seek another judge when God has sent down the detailed Book in truth. | terra: The Prophet asks whether he should seek a judge other than God when God has sent the Book fully explained; divine judgment and trusted revelation validate one another.

luna: This verse says the Lord's word is complete in truth and justice and cannot be changed, the stable divine speech set against the section's human fabrications and denial. | terra: The Lord’s word is completed in truth and justice and none can alter His words, combining reliable speech with settled finality.
terra: God opens the breast of the one guided to submission and makes the breast of the misled constricted; this concretizes the source section’s “broad breast” sense of balda.
luna: This verse commands full measure and weight in justice, then forbids reducing people's due; its continuation also commands just speech, binding honest measurement to honest words.

luna: The section develops both deceptive speech and a garment that misstates reality; this verse begins the Adam scene in which Satan's whisper aims to expose what had been covered, setting up the false oath and leaf-covering in 7:21–22.
luna: Satan swears that he is a sincere adviser, a direct false claim to trustworthiness; the next verse shows the deception's result.
luna: The verse says Satan deluded them, their nakedness became apparent, and they began covering themselves with leaves; it joins a false assurance to clothing that cannot conceal the truth.
luna: After the deception, Adam and his wife admit they wronged themselves and ask for mercy; their truthful confession reverses Satan's false assurance in the preceding verses.
luna: This verse names those who invent a lie against God or deny His signs, then says the angels take their souls; the false claim is placed within an eventual reckoning.
terra: The people of Paradise and Fire each confirm that they found their Lord’s promise true, and a caller judges the wrongdoers.
terra: Hud’s people say they think he is among the liars; his claim to be a trustworthy adviser in 7:68 directly answers this accusation.
terra: Hud denies being foolish and identifies himself as a messenger from the Lord; this clears the false personal charge in 7:66 before 7:68 asserts his trustworthiness.
terra: Hud calls himself “a trustworthy adviser,” showing amīn as the quality that warrants accepting admonitory speech.
luna: In another address to Midian, Shuayb commands full measure and weight and forbids depriving people of their due; this repeats the trustworthy messenger's concrete demand for truthful dealing.
terra: Shuʿayb asks God to judge truthfully between believers and deniers and calls Him the best of judges, placing divine حكم between accepted and rejected messenger-speech.
terra: True believers’ hearts tremble when God is mentioned, yet recited signs increase their faith and reliance; bodily awe marks a boundary rather than the wavering doubt opposed by the section.
terra: The angelic aid is only good news “so that your hearts may be reassured,” repeating the same promise-to-settled-heart relation in battle.

luna: During danger, God sends believers sleep as security, rain, and firmness for their hearts and feet; this concrete scene shows fear being removed and inward and bodily steadiness restored. | terra: God sends drowsiness as security from Him, cleanses the believers, binds their hearts, and makes their feet firm; inward and outward steadiness are one gift.
terra: God tells the angels that He is with them and commands them to make the believers firm, presenting divine presence as the answer to battlefield fear.

luna: The section defines amānah against betrayal; this warning names betrayal of God, the Messenger, and one's trusts as a knowing act, giving the opposite boundary of the reliable person. | terra: Believers are forbidden to betray God, the Messenger, or their trusts, exactly realizing the dictionary opposition between amānah and treachery.
terra: After the believers’ confidence in their numbers fails them and they turn back, God sends tranquility upon the Messenger and believers; divine calm arrests retreat.
terra: In the cave the Prophet says “Do not grieve; God is with us,” and God sends down tranquility, so a trusted reassurance becomes experienced calm.

luna: The section's dictionary gloss for ر د د describes repeated going and returning, and its gloss for ب ل د describes bewildered wavering; this verse says doubtful hearts “waver” (يَتَرَدَّدُونَ) within doubt, the direct opposite of settled trust. | terra: Those seeking exemption have doubting hearts and “waver in their doubt,” the explicit opposite of the settled heart implied by security and faith.
terra: The Prophet “believes in God and believes the believers,” using the same root first for faith and then for crediting people’s word; this directly exposes the section’s two linked senses.
terra: Breaking what they promised God and continuing to lie produces hypocrisy in their hearts, reversing the divine attribute of making a promise true.
terra: The builders of the harmful mosque swear that they intended only good, but God witnesses that they are liars; a pious-looking deed and its verbal defense are jointly false.
terra: After God’s covenantal promise to believers, the ayah asks who is more faithful to a covenant than God, closely matching the named divine sense of al-Muʾmin.

luna: The verse calls God's promise true, says all return to Him, and says He begins creation then repeats it; it binds fulfilled promise and divine making to the reckoning denied in the section. | terra: God’s true promise of universal return is grounded in His originating and repeating creation so that He may judge and reward justly.
terra: Those who do not expect the meeting with God become content and reassured by the nearer life; it is genuine settledness fixed on the wrong object.

luna: This verse puts the two sides of the section's question together: who is more unjust than one who invents a lie about God or denies His signs? It names both fabrication and rejection of truth. | terra: Inventing a lie against God and denying His signs are paired as the two gravest wrongs, joining fabricated speech to rejection of true speech.

luna: At the gathering, every soul is returned to God, its true Master, and the false objects it invoked disappear; this is a specific return for judgment that answers the section's wavering reliance and dīn theme.
terra: The question asks whether any alleged partner originates creation and repeats it; God alone does so, and the hearers are asked how they are turned away.
terra: One who guides to truth is contrasted with one unable to find the way without guidance, and the hearers are challenged over how they judge.
terra: Those who say the Qur’an was fabricated are challenged to produce one comparable surah and call witnesses if truthful.
terra: Asked whether the promised punishment is really true, the Prophet answers by his Lord that it is certainly true and inescapable.
terra: The ayah declares that God’s promise is true even though most people do not know, setting objective reliability against unsettled human recognition.

luna: The verse says God's allies will have no fear and will not grieve; this is a direct assurance of fear removed, the section's stated root sense of security. | terra: God’s allies have no fear or grief; 10:63 identifies them as believers, and 10:64 grounds their security in God’s unchangeable word.

luna: The next verse identifies those allies as people who believe and are mindful of God, specifying the faith behind the assurance in 10:62. | terra: The secure people of 10:62 are specifically those who believed and were mindful, while 10:64 supplies the reliable promise behind their state.

luna: Their good news is promised in this life and the Hereafter, and God's words cannot change; this makes the security of 10:62 rest on a reliable promise. | terra: For the believing friends of God, His words cannot be changed; this grounds the good news and freedom from fear stated in 10:62–63.

luna: The Prophet is told to follow the revelation, wait patiently until God judges, and trust that He is the best judge; this directly connects the reliable message with the section's final appeal to God's judgment. | terra: The Prophet is told to follow revelation and wait patiently until God judges, with God named the best of judges; trustworthy reception culminates in His decision.
terra: The Book’s signs are “made firm” (أُحْكِمَتْ) and then detailed by the Wise, directly applying the firmness sense of حكم to trustworthy revelation.

luna: The deniers call the Quran fabricated and are challenged to bring ten fabricated surahs like it; the challenge tests the very boundary between invented speech and revelation. | terra: The claim that the Prophet fabricated the Qur’an is met by a challenge to produce ten comparable surahs and enlist any available helpers.
luna: The continuation says that if they cannot answer, they should know the Quran was sent down with God's knowledge; it supplies the true source against the fabrication accusation in 11:13.
terra: Noah invokes God as “the wisest of judges” while appealing to a promise; God’s ruling in the next ayah clarifies rather than breaks the promise.
terra: Messenger-stories are related to make the Prophet’s heart firm, and in them truth, admonition, and reminder arrive together.

luna: The section uses Yusuf's brothers' claim in 12:17 to show how belief can be withheld; two verses earlier they ask why Jacob does not trust them with Yusuf (لَا تَأْمَنَّا), setting up the very trust their actions betray. | terra: Joseph’s brothers ask their father why he does not trust them with Joseph; their later false report in 12:17–18 exposes the requested trust as betrayed.

luna: The brothers promise to guard Yusuf and say he will enjoy himself; this assurance is the specific speech that their later act and wolf story falsify, making the section's trust-versus-lying-in-deed distinction concrete.

luna: Jacob says Yusuf's going away will grieve him and fears a wolf may eat him while they are unaware; the next events show his fear was warranted and expose the brothers' confident promise as false.
luna: The brothers answer Jacob that their strong group would be losers if a wolf ate Yusuf; their own group abandons him, so the verse records a confident assurance contradicted by the deed.
luna: After promising protection, the brothers put Yusuf in the bottom of a well; this betrayal is the acted falsehood that the section says can accompany lying in speech.

luna: The brothers return at night weeping after the betrayal; their performed grief adds a false outward display to the false account that follows, matching the section's point that a state or action can lie.

luna: The section explicitly cites the brothers' words ما أنت بمؤمن لنا ولو كنا صادقين: they pre-empt belief in their report even while claiming truth, and then blame the wolf, staging the conflict between trust and false testimony. | terra: Joseph’s brothers concede, “you will not believe us, even if we are truthful,” making belief precisely the acceptance of a speaker’s truthfulness.

luna: The section's dictionary entry for ك ذ ب calls a dyed cloth that looks embroidered a garment that “lies by its state”; here the brothers stain Yusuf's shirt with false blood as proof of their fabricated wolf story. | terra: The brothers bring Joseph’s shirt with “false blood” (بِدَمٍ كَذِبٍ); a fabric’s visible state participates in a lie, closely enacting the section’s deceptive-cloth sense.

luna: The section's secondary dictionary entry for ك ذ ب says a decorated cloth can “lie by its state”; after the attempted seduction, this verse records the tearing of Joseph's shirt from behind, introducing the garment evidence developed in 12:26–28.

luna: The section's secondary gloss calls deceptive cloth a surface that misstates what happened; in this later Yusuf scene, his answer to the adultery charge is tested by the shirt's tear, so the garment can expose rather than conceal a lie. | terra: A witness makes the direction of the tear in Joseph’s shirt adjudicate whether the woman is truthful and Joseph a liar; the cloth itself becomes evidence about speech.

luna: This witness says that a shirt torn from behind would show that the woman lied and Yusuf spoke truth; the shirt's physical state distinguishes the competing claims, a precise reversal of the section's deceptive-cloth image. | terra: The shirt torn from behind proves that the woman lied and Joseph told the truth, reversing the deceptive shirt of 12:18 into fabric that discloses reality.

luna: When the husband sees the shirt torn from behind, he calls the accusation a plot; the fabric here tells the truth about the action, countering the section's dictionary example of fabric that lies by appearance.
terra: After Joseph’s truthfulness has been disclosed, the king declares him established and trustworthy, making tested speech the ground of entrusted office.
terra: Jacob asks whether he should entrust Benjamin to the brothers as he entrusted Joseph before, making remembered betrayal govern renewed confidence.

luna: The section's dictionary gloss for د ي ن connects the root with trust in judgment; in this Yusuf episode, دِينِ الْمَلِكِ means the king's legal order, a distinct but concrete legal sense of the same root. | terra: Joseph’s plan proceeds under “the king’s law” (دِينِ ٱلْمَلِكِ), showing dīn in a judicial order rather than only the eschatological object denied in 95:7.
terra: Joseph’s eldest brother vows not to leave the land until his father permits him or God judges; remaining in place and waiting for divine حكم unite the section’s two final dictionary images.
terra: Joseph tells his family to enter Egypt secure, closing a story driven by betrayed trust with safe reunion under his verified word.

luna: The section says the root sense of security is tranquility and fear's departure; here believing hearts find tranquility (تَطْمَئِنُّ الْقُلُوبُ) in God's remembrance. | terra: Believing hearts find reassurance in God’s remembrance, explicitly stating the section’s definition of security as inward settledness.
luna: At judgment, Satan admits “I promised you, then failed you” while God's promise was true; this reverses the section's description of Allah as al-Muʾmin, the fulfiller of His promise.

luna: The section's title joins a trusted word to a settled heart; here God makes firm those who believe with the firm word in worldly life and the Hereafter, directly coupling belief with steadfastness. | terra: God makes those who believe firm through “the firm word” (ٱلْقَوْلِ ٱلثَّابِتِ), directly joining accepted speech to settledness.

luna: Ibrahim again asks that Mecca be made بَلَدًا آمِنًا; this is a direct parallel to the section's “secure city” and locates security in a prayer to God. | terra: Abraham again asks, “make this city secure,” tying the demonstrative city to security and protection from false worship.
terra: The Prophet must not think God will fail His promise to His messengers; divine vindication is guaranteed despite present denial.
terra: The people of the Garden are told to enter in peace and security, making removed fear a final settled condition.

luna: The verse asks whether the One who creates is like what does not create; it states the actual-making distinction that the section raises between God's creation and human fabrication. | terra: “Is one who creates like one who does not create?” draws the exact boundary between real making and objects falsely treated as makers.

luna: The verse says God gives life and then returns some people to the weakest age after knowledge; this is a specific bodily lowering that echoes 95:5's return to the lowest condition, though the two passages do not define that condition identically.

luna: The verse commands people to fulfill God's covenant and not break confirmed oaths, noting that God is their guarantor; this is a concrete human counterpart to the section's note that al-Muʾmin is the One who fulfills His promise.
luna: When a revelation is substituted for another, opponents say “you are only a fabricator”; this is the section's exact pattern of accusing a truthful messenger of invention.

luna: The reply says the Holy Spirit brought revelation down in truth to make believers firm; this directly answers the accusation in 16:101 and links trusted transmission with firmness. | terra: The Holy Spirit brings the Qur’an down in truth to make those who believe firm, joining a reliable carrier, a true word, faith, and settledness in one ayah.

luna: The next objection is that a human teaches the Prophet; the verse answers that the alleged teacher's language is foreign while the Quran is clear Arabic, giving the concrete basis of the dispute over its source.
luna: The verse says those who invent falsehood are the ones who do not believe God's signs; it reverses the deniers' charge and identifies fabrication with their own lack of faith.

luna: The section's root gloss for ء م ن makes faith true assent and security a settled heart; this verse makes a precise exception for a coerced denial when the heart remains secure in faith, distinguishing an utterance from inward belief. | terra: A person coerced into an outward word of unbelief remains excepted when the heart is “secure in faith” (مُطْمَئِنٌّۢ بِٱلْإِيمَٰنِ), separating verbal appearance from inward truth.

luna: The section's city is al-amīn, secure; this verse describes a town that was safe and settled (آمِنَةً مُّطْمَئِنَّةً) but lost that state through ingratitude, a specific reversal of security into fear and hunger. | terra: A town once secure and inwardly at ease rejects God’s favors, so God clothes it in hunger and fear; security, denial, garment, and fear reverse within one image.
terra: A messenger from the secure town’s own people comes, but they call him a liar; punishment then seizes them, explaining the reversal narrated in 16:112.
terra: People are forbidden to let their tongues falsely label things lawful or unlawful and thereby fabricate a lie against God; speech itself manufactures the false religious claim.
luna: This verse commands fulfillment of a covenant and says the covenant will be asked about; it joins trustworthiness in a promise to later accountability.
luna: The verse commands full measure and weighing with a straight balance, directly countering the measure fraud that the section connects with denial of the Day.
terra: God tells the Prophet that divine strengthening kept him from inclining toward the pressure of opponents, marking firmness as protection against even a slight turn.
luna: The Quran says that even if humans and jinn gathered to produce its like, they could not; this gives a concrete test of the claim that revelation is merely manufactured speech.
terra: God strengthens the youths’ hearts when they stand and declare their Lord, joining an anchored heart to courageous truthful speech.

luna: The companions of the cave say their people have taken other gods and ask for clear authority; “who is more unjust than one who invents a lie about God?” makes fabricated worship claims a specific case of false making.
terra: Discovery of the sleepers is arranged so people may know that God’s promise is true and the Hour admits no doubt; an observed sign settles contested speech.
terra: The Prophet must recite what is revealed because none can alter God’s words, presenting the divine utterance as fixed and dependable.
terra: Moses says he will not cease until reaching the meeting of the two seas; persistence and water give a concrete parallel to the source dictionary’s animals that do not leave the pool.
terra: The unseen Gardens promised by the Merciful are assured because His promise is bound to arrive.
terra: Moses asks, “expand for me my breast,” so that he can deliver his difficult speech; an opened chest supports a trustworthy messenger’s utterance.
terra: Moses and Aaron are told not to fear because God is with them, hearing and seeing; the trusted divine assurance answers their apprehension before speaking to Pharaoh.
terra: The calf-worshippers say they will not cease clinging to it until Moses returns; steadfast nondeparture is attached to a false object, reversing the section’s desired fixed answer.
luna: Satan offers Adam the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay; this is a specific promise that misleads, opposite to the section's description of the One who makes His promise true.

luna: After eating, Adam and his wife become aware of their nakedness and cover themselves with leaves; the bodily result completes the false promise in 20:120 and echoes the section's deceptive-cloth discussion.
luna: On the Day of Resurrection, God sets just balances so no soul is wronged, even by a mustard seed's weight; this concretely answers the dishonest measuring associated with denial in 83.
terra: God promises to repeat creation as He began it and says the promise is binding upon Him and will be done, uniting true making with fulfilled speech.

luna: The section opposes a settled heart to wavering trust; this person worships God at the edge, feels reassured when good comes, but turns back when tested, an explicit reversal of stable faith. | terra: The edge-worshipper is reassured by benefit but turns completely when tested, portraying a conditional calm that never becomes rooted faith.
luna: When the wavering worshipper in 22:11 turns, this verse says he calls on what can neither harm nor benefit him; that ineffective refuge completes the consequence of unstable trust.
luna: The continuation calls that invoked object a harmful patron and companion; it shows where the unstable reliance of 22:11–12 leads, not merely that the person changes stance.
terra: God removes what Satan casts into prophetic recitation and then makes His signs firm; 22:54 shows knowledge, faith, and humbled hearts as the result.
terra: What Satan casts becomes a trial for diseased and hardened hearts; this row supplies the unstable recipients contrasted with the knowing, believing hearts of 22:54.
terra: Those given knowledge recognize revelation as truth, believe it, and let their hearts yield to it; this is the heart’s response to God making His signs firm in 22:52.
luna: This verse says God will judge between people on the Day of Resurrection over their disagreements, an explicit instance of the judgment the section associates with dīn.

luna: The section's word emīn means a trustworthy person; this description of successful believers says they keep their trusts and covenants, showing trustworthiness in conduct rather than only a title. | terra: The believers guard their trusts and covenants, giving action as the proof of the reliability named by amānah.
luna: The Quran describes human creation from an essence of clay; the section's question of actual divine creation versus fabrication has a concrete account of the human's origin.
luna: The next verse places the human seed in a secure resting place; it adds the protected beginning of the bodily process described in 23:12–14.
luna: The verse follows the stages of formation and calls God the best of creators; it directly supports the section's image of the human made in excellent form.
luna: After detailing creation, the next verse says humans will die; it begins the passage's movement from created life toward the return relevant to the section's question about dīn.
luna: The continuation says people will be raised on the Day of Resurrection, completing the creation, death, and judgment sequence.
terra: At death the wrongdoer asks to be returned, supplying the requested reversal whose asserted purpose appears in 23:100.
terra: The plea to return and act righteously is refused as “only a word he says,” exposing a late promise whose speech cannot establish trust.
terra: The slanderers’ failure to produce four witnesses means that before God they are the liars, showing a false report judged by an evidentiary standard.
terra: People say “we believe and obey,” then a group turns away, so conduct refuses the word their mouths accepted.

luna: The section's gloss for د ي ن connects trust with judgment; here people called to Allah and the Messenger for judgment turn away, a concrete refusal of the trustworthy ruling the section sets against assent. | terra: When called to God and the Messenger for judgment, a group turns away; the ayah makes rejection of the judge the action behind 24:47’s false profession.

luna: The section contrasts accepting a word with rejecting its speaker; this continuation says they come submissively when the ruling favors them, exposing selective rather than settled acceptance. | terra: When the judgment favors them, the same refusers come obediently; this selective acceptance exposes the instability diagnosed in 24:50.

luna: The section describes doubt as a heart that wanders; this question names disease, doubt, and fear of injustice as reasons for refusing judgment, completing the scene begun in 24:48. | terra: The refusers are asked whether their hearts are diseased, they doubt, or they fear injustice from God and His Messenger; unstable heart and distrust of judgment coincide.

luna: The section's iman gloss is tasdīq, accepting a true word; the believers' answer here is “we hear and obey” when summoned for judgment, the settled response opposite to the turning away in 24:48. | terra: The believers’ stable response when called for judgment is simply “we hear and we obey,” the accepting counterpart to 24:47–50.

luna: The section joins faith, good action, and lasting reward; this continuation associates obedience to Allah and His Messenger, fear of God, and piety with success, explaining the stance shown in 24:51.
terra: God promises believers that He will replace their fear with security; the divine promise itself bears the meaning attributed to al-Muʾmin.

luna: Opponents say the Quran is only a lie the Prophet invented and that others helped him; this directly stages the accusation of fabricated revelation named by the section. | terra: The unbelievers call the Qur’an a lie invented with others’ help; the ayah itself judges that accusation an unjust falsehood.
luna: They specify that the supposed invention is old tales written down and recited; the verse gives a concrete form to the accusation in 25:4.
luna: The answer says the Quran was sent down by the One who knows the secret of the heavens and earth; this is the true source set against the fabrication claim of 25:4–5.
terra: The Qur’an is revealed gradually to strengthen the Prophet’s heart, so the trustworthy word itself produces inward steadiness.
luna: On the Day when wealth and children will not help, only the one who comes to God with a sound heart will benefit; this gives the section's settled heart a specific role at judgment.

luna: The section notes that messengers who call themselves trustworthy are answered with denial; this passage says Noah's people denied the messengers, the rejection that frames his “trustworthy messenger” claim in 26:107. | terra: Noah’s people deny the messengers; this row supplies the rejecting response to the trustworthy self-identification in 26:107.

luna: The section names emīn as trustworthy; Noah tells his people إِنِّي لَكُمْ رَسُولٌ أَمِينٌ, so the precise title is used by the messenger whose warning is under dispute. | terra: Noah introduces himself to his deniers as “a trustworthy messenger,” the exact messenger formula developed by the section.
terra: Immediately after Noah calls himself trustworthy, he commands his people to be mindful of God and obey him; the ayah states the response that amānah warrants.
terra: ʿĀd deny the messengers, providing the rejection to which Hud’s claim of trustworthiness in 26:125 answers.

luna: Hud repeats the section's exact title رَسُولٌ أَمِينٌ to his people, identifying himself as a trustworthy carrier before urging them to fear God and obey in the next verse. | terra: Hud repeats “I am to you a trustworthy messenger,” showing that trustworthiness belongs to the recurring office, not merely one personality.
terra: Hud’s trustworthy-messenger declaration is followed by the repeated demand for obedience, making confidence in the bearer practical.
terra: Deniers dismiss the warning as “nothing but khuluq of the former peoples”; the disputed sense of خُلُق/خَلْق matters because inherited pattern is used to neutralize a true warning.
terra: Thamud deny the messengers, forming the denial half of the trust-and-rejection scene completed in 26:143.

luna: Salih uses the same “trustworthy messenger” wording رَسُولٌ أَمِينٌ; the repeated self-description shows that reliability is attached to the messenger's call, not a claim unique to Noah. | terra: Ṣāliḥ gives the same “trustworthy messenger” self-description before delivering his demand for obedience.
terra: Ṣāliḥ follows his claim of trustworthiness with a command to heed and obey, distinguishing accepted messenger-speech from his people’s denial.
terra: Thamud are asked whether they expect to be left secure amid their gardens; their felt safety stands opposite their denial of the trustworthy messenger in 26:141–143.

luna: The section's secondary dictionary entry for ل ي س pictures camels that stay by a water basin and do not leave; Salih's she-camel is assigned a known drinking day here, a specific but indirect water-and-camel echo.
terra: Lot’s people deny the messengers; 26:162 separately answers that denial with the messenger’s trustworthy status.

luna: Lot likewise calls himself رَسُولٌ أَمِينٌ before warning his people; this is another direct occurrence of the section's messenger-trust formulation. | terra: Lot identifies himself as a trustworthy messenger, again locating amānah in the bearer of the divine word.
terra: Lot’s declaration of amānah leads directly to the command to obey, giving the trusted word its demanded reception.
terra: The people of the thicket deny the messengers, supplying the response against which 26:178 asserts trustworthiness.

luna: Shuayb uses the same exact title رَسُولٌ أَمِينٌ before telling his people to fear God and obey him, completing the repeated messenger pattern the section describes. | terra: Shuʿayb repeats the trustworthy-messenger formula, here before a people whose practice also falsifies measure.
terra: Shuʿayb’s trustworthy status likewise grounds the call to obey, completing the final repetition of the scene.
luna: The Shuayb who calls himself a trustworthy messenger in 26:178 commands his people here to give full measure; the passage joins the reliable messenger's word to honest dealing.
luna: Shuayb continues by commanding just weighing; this supplies the second side of fair trade in the same speech begun at 26:181.
luna: The same address forbids depriving people of their due and spreading corruption, completing Shuayb's specific contrast between honest conduct and betrayal.
luna: Shuayb grounds the command in fearing the One who created them and earlier peoples; this connects the trade warning to its Creator and Judge.

luna: The section identifies the Spirit as a trustworthy carrier of revelation; this immediately preceding verse names the Quran as a sending-down from the Lord of the worlds, the source that 26:193's carrier conveys.

luna: The section explicitly cites نَزَلَ بِهِ الرُّوحُ الْأَمِينُ: the trustworthy Spirit brings revelation, giving the divine message a reliable bearer. | terra: The trustworthy Spirit brings the revelation down, extending reliability from the human messenger to the message’s heavenly carrier.
luna: The next verse says the revelation came down upon Muhammad's heart so he would be among the warners; it completes the passage's path from trustworthy carrier to receiving heart.
terra: At the staff’s movement Moses turns fleeing and does not look back, and God answers the flight with “Do not fear,” repeating the boundary between panic and divine security.
terra: The jinn offers to bring the throne and says he is strong and trustworthy for the task, making amānah reliability in carrying out a promised act.
terra: One who brings a good deed is safe from the terror of the Judgment Day, placing true security on the far side of accountable action.
terra: Moses’ mother nearly discloses him, but God binds her heart so that she may remain among the believers; firmness preserves faith under fear.
terra: Moses is restored to his mother so that her eye may be comforted, she may cease grieving, and she may know God’s promise is true; it completes the heart-strengthening act of 28:10.
terra: The woman recommends Moses as strong and trustworthy after observing his conduct, so the character judgment rests on deed rather than self-display.

luna: The section's secondary dictionary gloss for ك ذ ب describes a wild creature running and stopping to look behind; Moses here turns in flight and does not look back, then is called “approach, and do not fear” and told he is among the secure, reversing flight into safety. | terra: Moses flees without looking back, unlike the source-section animal that stops to look behind; he is then called forward and told not to fear because he is safe.
luna: After calling Moses back and assuring him in 28:31, God gives him two signs and tells him to go to Pharaoh; the secure return becomes a commission rather than continued retreat.
terra: The objection that following guidance would cause abduction is answered by God’s establishment of a secure sanctuary, exposing fear as resistance to a trustworthy word.
terra: People are not left merely to say “we believe” without trial; the spoken profession must be tested.
terra: Trial makes manifest those who are truthful and those who lie, supplying the verdict on the profession stated in 29:2.
terra: A person says “we believe” but reverses under human persecution; the closing question asks whether God is not best aware of what hearts contain.

luna: The section explicitly cites إبراهيم's وَتَخْلُقُونَ إِفْكًا; its dictionary gloss for خ ل ق describes fabricating and shaping a lie in the mind, so this verse is the exact false-making claim set against God's creation. | terra: Abraham tells his people that they “create a falsehood” (تَخْلُقُونَ إِفْكًا), the exact named sense in which creating becomes fabricating.

luna: Ibrahim's next words say that if they deny him, earlier peoples denied messengers too and the messenger's duty is clear delivery; this joins the fabricated claim in 29:17 to rejection of a trusted speaker.

luna: After the verse about fabricating falsehood, Ibrahim asks whether people have not seen how God begins creation then repeats it; the passage directly distinguishes divine making from human fabrication. | terra: Soon after Abraham names fabricated falsehood in 29:17, this ayah asks whether people see how God originates creation, locally setting actual creation against invention.

luna: The next verse tells people to travel the earth and observe how creation began; it develops the reality of God's making that stands against the fabricated objects and claims in 29:17–19. | terra: The command to travel and observe how creation began extends 29:19’s answer to the fabricated objects and stories rejected in 29:17.

luna: This verse contrasts the secure sanctuary God made for Mecca with people being snatched away around it, yet its residents believe falsehood and deny God's favor; safety does not itself ensure truthful faith. | terra: People see God make a secure sanctuary amid surrounding abduction, yet believe in falsehood and reject His favor; received safety does not settle their assent.

luna: This verse asks who is more unjust than one who invents a lie about God or denies the truth when it reaches him; that is the section's distinction between fabricated accusation and genuine revelation.
terra: “God’s promise—God does not fail His promise” states in repeated form the reliability attributed to the divine name al-Muʾmin.
luna: God begins creation and then repeats it, and people will be returned to Him; this joins true creation, return, and judgment in the order the section's verses set out.
luna: God originates creation and repeats it, and the verse says this is easy for Him; it is another explicit formulation of the actual creation and return that answer denial in the section.
terra: “This is God’s creation; show Me what those besides Him created” sets actual making against unsupported claims for rivals.
terra: One who submits to God while doing good has grasped the firmest handhold; trust becomes settled reliance with enacted goodness.
terra: God’s promise is true, while worldly life and the deceiver can delude; dependable word is set against misleading appearance and speech.
terra: The accusation “he fabricated it” is rejected with the statement that it is truth from the Lord, sent to warn a previously unwarned people.
luna: The deniers ask whether they will really be created anew after being lost in the earth and then deny meeting their Lord; this is a direct objection to renewed creation and accountability.
luna: The angel of death takes people and they are returned to their Lord; this literal return supplies a judgment scene for the section's repeated ر د د motif.
terra: In the crisis hypocrites and diseased hearts say God and His Messenger promised only delusion; 33:22 answers with the believers’ declaration that both spoke true.
terra: When the believers see the confederates, the feared event verifies God’s and the Messenger’s promise; they answer “God and His Messenger spoke true,” and their faith increases.

luna: The verse describes believers who kept their covenant with God: some fulfilled their vow and some still await, without changing their commitment; it gives a specific human form of the section's trustworthiness.
terra: Once God and His Messenger decide a matter, a believer has no residual choice, giving the settled form of accepting authoritative judgment.

luna: The section says lying occurs in speech and deed; this command to speak a straight, sound word is followed by God's promise to set deeds right, a specific opposite link between words and actions.

luna: The section defines amānah as trustworthiness against betrayal; here the cosmic trust is offered to the heavens, earth, and mountains, then borne by the human, whom the verse calls unjust and ignorant, a boundary between receiving a trust and proving reliable in it. | terra: The Trust is offered to creation and borne by the human being, enlarging amānah from an interpersonal deposit into a weighty moral charge.
terra: Those who disbelieve say the Hour will not come; the Prophet answers “Yes, by my Lord,” grounding the fixed response in God’s knowledge.
luna: The opponents mock the claim that people will be created anew after disintegration; this is the resurrection dispute to which the next verse's accusation of invention responds.
luna: The opponents call the warning either a lie invented against God or madness; the verse directly combines fabricated speech with the coming claim of resurrection.
luna: The next verse asks whether they do not see what lies before and behind them of heaven and earth; it answers the mockery of renewed creation in 34:7 with visible created reality.
luna: When clear signs are recited, the disbelievers call the message “nothing but a fabricated lie”; this is another direct rejection of a true message as invention.
terra: “God’s promise is true” is followed by warnings against being deceived by worldly life or the deceiver, setting reliable promise against misleading appearance.
terra: At resurrection the sleepers recognize, “This is what the Merciful promised, and the messengers spoke truth,” so the once-contested promise publicly vindicates its speakers.

luna: Whoever is given long life is reversed in creation, the verse says; this is a concrete bodily reversal relevant to 95:5's “returning” language, without requiring that the passages mean the same final state.

luna: The verse reminds humans that God created them from a drop, then notes that they become open disputants; it joins actual creation to the very posture of denial challenged in the section. | terra: The human created from a drop becomes an open adversary, staging true creation as the basis that should have prevented argumentative denial.

luna: A man asks who can revive bones after they have crumbled; this is a direct denial of resurrection following the dispute about human creation. | terra: The objector forgets his own creation and produces a challenge about reviving bones, turning createdness into a fabricated argument against return.

luna: The answer is that the One who originated them the first time will revive them; it grounds resurrection in the real creation that the section contrasts with fabricated claims. | terra: The answer appeals to the One who created the bones the first time, identifying the real Maker against the human’s denying speech in 36:78.

luna: The next argument asks whether the One who created the heavens and earth cannot create people like them; it extends the first-creation proof from bones to the whole world. | terra: “Is not” the Creator of the heavens and earth able to recreate them? “Yes” makes the stable response explicit and names Him the all-knowing Creator.
luna: God's command when He wills a thing is only to say “Be,” and it is; this states how the Creator's act differs from human verbal invention.
luna: The surah closes by declaring sovereignty belongs to the One in whose hand is the dominion of all things and to whom people return; this completes the creation-and-accountability argument.
luna: Ibrahim is described as coming to his Lord with a sound heart; this is a second Quranic formulation of the sound heart that 26:89 makes decisive at judgment.
luna: Ibrahim asks his people whether they worship what they carve with their own hands; this is a specific confrontation between made objects and the real Creator.
luna: The next verse says God created them and what they make, completing Ibrahim's contrast between their manufactured idols and divine creation.

luna: The section explicitly quotes the deniers' claim إِنْ هَٰذَا إِلَّا اخْتِلَاقٌ about revelation; this is a direct accusation that the true message is an invention. | terra: The chiefs dismiss the proclamation of one God as nothing but fabrication (ٱخْتِلَٰقٌ), falsely assigning inventedness to revelation.
luna: The next verse shows their objection more specifically: why was the Reminder sent down to him from among them? It completes the social challenge behind calling revelation fabricated in 38:7.
terra: The promised lofty chambers are guaranteed with the statement that God does not fail the appointed promise.
terra: A breast opened to submission and illuminated by the Lord is contrasted with hardened hearts, developing the section’s broad-chest image into receptive faith.
terra: The best discourse first makes skins shiver, then skins and hearts soften to God’s remembrance; agitation resolves into receptive rest rather than indecision.

luna: The verse again joins lying about God with denying truth when it comes, then asks whether Hell is not the disbelievers' home; it connects the section's fabrication/denial contrast to judgment. | terra: One person invents a lie against God and also denies the truth when it arrives, bringing fabrication and rejection into the same act.

luna: Against the liar and denier named in 39:32, this verse describes the one who brings truth and the one who confirms it as God-conscious; it supplies the faithful response opposite to fabrication. | terra: The one who brings truth and the one who confirms it (وَصَدَّقَ بِهِ) form the positive pair of trustworthy word and believing reception.
terra: “Is God not sufficient for His servant?” demands a settled yes while others try to frighten the Prophet, matching the secure answer sought by 95:8.

luna: At the Resurrection, the book is set, prophets and witnesses are brought, and God judges between people with truth so none are wronged; it supplies a concrete scene for the section's dīn and divine-judge themes. | terra: At the final gathering the record is set down, prophets and witnesses are brought, and judgment is made in truth, publicly resolving contested testimony.
terra: The people of Paradise praise God for making His promise true, presenting fulfillment as the public verification of the trusted divine word.
terra: God judges with truth, whereas the beings invoked besides Him cannot judge anything; real judgment is distinguished from an empty attribution.

luna: A believer from Pharaoh's household argues that if Moses is lying, the lie is on him, but if he is truthful Pharaoh will face part of his warning; this is a concrete test of how to assess the trustworthy messenger's word. | terra: Pharaoh’s believing kinsman weighs Moses’ claim: if Moses lies, the lie returns upon him, but if he is truthful, some promised consequence will strike; trusting a messenger is framed as a testable judgment.
terra: The Prophet is told to be patient because God’s promise is true, so steadiness rests upon confidence in the divine word.
luna: This verse says God made the earth a resting place, formed people, and made their forms beautiful; the phrasing directly parallels the section's human made in excellent form.

luna: The verse traces human life from dust through birth and maturity to old age, with some dying earlier; it gives a specific bodily decline that echoes 95:5's return to a low state, though it does not define that state identically.
terra: Whether the Prophet sees part of the threatened outcome or dies first, what God promises the deniers will come, making fulfillment independent of the hearer’s timetable.

luna: Those who say “our Lord is God” and then stand firm receive angels' reassurance not to fear or grieve and the promise of Paradise; this is the section's stable trust and fear removed in a single scene. | terra: Those who say “Our Lord is God” and then remain upright are told not to fear and are given the promised Garden; stable word and removed fear coincide.
luna: The angels continue by saying they are believers' protectors in worldly life and the Hereafter; this completes the reassurance begun in 41:30 with protection across both lives.
luna: The angels identify this reassurance as hospitality from the Forgiving, Merciful One, completing the promised welcome that follows the firm confession in 41:30.
terra: The one cast into Fire is set against the one who arrives secure on Resurrection Day, making final judgment the boundary between apparent impunity and real safety.

luna: The section's dictionary gloss for د ي ن includes trusting someone in judgment; this verse assigns disputed judgment to God and immediately says “upon Him I rely,” joining true adjudication to trust in the Judge.

luna: When opponents say the Prophet invented a lie about God, this verse answers that God blots out falsehood and establishes truth by His words, directly resolving the section's question about real making and invention. | terra: The accusation that the Prophet fabricated a lie is answered by God’s effacing falsehood and confirming truth with His words; fabricated and established speech are expressly separated.

luna: Moses tells Pharaoh إِنِّي لَكُمْ رَسُولٌ أَمِينٌ, the same exact trustworthy-messenger title the section finds repeated among the messengers in 26. | terra: Moses addresses Pharaoh’s people as “a trustworthy messenger,” making his demand rest explicitly on the speaker’s reliability.

luna: Moses follows his trustworthy-messenger claim in 44:18 by telling Pharaoh not to exalt himself against God and saying he has clear authority; this states the warning carried by that reliable speaker.
terra: After naming himself a trustworthy messenger in 44:18, Moses says, “If you do not believe me, then leave me alone”; the cited ayah makes personal trust in the messenger the contested response.
terra: The mindful are placed in a secure station, carrying the “remaining in a trusted place” side of the image into the final abode.
luna: These people say there is only worldly life and deny being raised after death; this is a concrete rejection of the judgment and return whose denial the section asks what could justify.
luna: When God's signs are recited, their only argument is to demand that their fathers be brought back if they are truthful; it makes their refusal of resurrection a challenge to the message.
luna: The answer says God gives life and causes death, then gathers people for the Day of Resurrection; it supplies the divine power and appointed judgment denied in 45:24–25.

luna: Asked whether the Prophet invented the message, the answer says that if he had, no one could protect him from God; the accusation is placed under the judgment of the One who knows and witnesses. | terra: When opponents say the revelation was fabricated, the Prophet is told to acknowledge that fabrication would leave him helpless before God; God knows their hostile discourse.
terra: Those who say “Our Lord is God” and remain upright have no fear or grief, closely joining settled commitment to the root meaning of security.
terra: After recalling creation of the heavens and earth, the ayah asks whether God is not able to revive the dead and supplies “Yes” as the fixed response.
terra: Believers who support God’s cause are promised divine support and firmly planted feet, rendering faithful commitment as stability in action.
terra: When a decisive surah (سُورَةٌ مُّحْكَمَةٌ) names fighting, diseased hearts look with deathly fear; a firm word reveals an unsteady interior.
terra: Obedience and proper speech are demanded, but when the matter is resolved, truthfulness to God would be better; the testing act exposes the earlier words.

luna: This verse says God sent tranquility into believers' hearts so their faith would increase; it makes the section's link between faith and a calm, secure heart explicit. | terra: God sends tranquility into believers’ hearts so that they increase in faith, directly joining sakīnah, heart, and īmān.
luna: The pledge to the Prophet is described as a pledge to God, whose hand is over theirs; whoever fulfills it receives a great reward, making loyalty to a trusted messenger an accountable act.
terra: Those who stayed behind “say with their tongues what is not in their hearts,” a precise instance of the section’s lie in both utterance and act.

luna: After the pledge beneath the tree, God sends tranquility into the believers' hearts; the named inward settling follows a concrete act of allegiance and trust. | terra: God knows what is in the pledgers’ hearts and sends tranquility upon them, joining tested loyalty, inward knowledge, and settledness.
terra: Against pagan zeal, God sends tranquility upon His Messenger and believers and binds them to the word of piety; calm and a binding word answer agitation.

luna: The promised return to the Sacred Mosque is explicitly “in safety” (آمِنِينَ); this connects secure entry into Mecca with the section's city and its assurance of safety. | terra: God verifies His Messenger’s true vision by promising entry into the Sacred Mosque “secure” and without fear, joining a fulfilled divine word to safety.

luna: The section labels the root ء م ن's iman sense as tasdīq and links security to a settled heart; this verse corrects people who say “we believe”: faith has not entered their hearts, so their spoken claim is not yet inward assent. | terra: The Bedouins’ verbal “we believe” is corrected because faith has not entered their hearts, directly separating a claim of belief from inward assent.

luna: After distinguishing mere profession in 49:14, this verse describes true believers as those who believe and then do not doubt; that untroubled heart directly answers the section's picture of trust as calmness. | terra: True believers are those who believe and then do not doubt, defining faith by the absence of the oscillation displayed in 9:45.
luna: The deniers' doubt about renewed creation is met by the question whether the first creation wearied God; this directly uses original making to answer denial of a new creation.
terra: At judgment God states that the word is not changed in His presence and that He does not wrong servants; finality of speech and justice coincide.

luna: The opponents say the Prophet has invented the Quran; this is a direct instance of the false-making charge developed in the section. | terra: The charge that the Prophet composed the revelation is answered, “Rather, they do not believe,” making alleged fabrication a form of refused faith.

luna: The next verse challenges them to produce a statement like it if they are truthful, testing the invented-speech claim rather than leaving it as a shared accusation. | terra: Those alleging invented speech are challenged to produce a discourse like it “if they are truthful”; this ayah tests the speakers of the charge made in 52:33.

luna: Immediately after the challenge, the Quran asks whether they were created from nothing or are themselves creators; this makes the section's question about God's actual creation versus a fabricated claim explicit. | terra: “Were they created from nothing, or are they the creators?” forces denial back onto the question of which making is real.
luna: The next question asks whether they created the heavens and earth; it extends 52:35's creator question from human beings to the world that witnesses to its Maker.
terra: “The heart did not lie about what it saw” (مَا كَذَبَ ٱلْفُؤَادُ), bringing the lying root directly into a claim about the heart’s faithful witness.

luna: The section's secondary entry for ل ي س is the camel that stays at the trough; this nearby account divides the water between the people and the she-camel, a plausible but uncertain echo of that dictionary scene.
luna: The verse says God raised the heaven and set the balance; it locates the standard behind the fair weights that the section contrasts with cheating.
luna: The next verse forbids transgressing the balance, marking the boundary against the cheating in measure named by the section.
luna: The continuation commands establishing weight with justice and not making the balance deficient, completing the fair-measure scene.
terra: The hypocrites admit that they tempted themselves, waited, doubted, and were deceived by wishes until God’s command came, tracing an unsettled heart into fatal false confidence.
terra: Believers are called to let their hearts become humble to God’s remembrance and the revealed truth, making the true word’s inward effect the issue.

luna: The section's dictionary note reads the divine name al-Muʾmin as the One who makes good His promise to His servant; this verse names God الْمُؤْمِنُ among His attributes, placing that assurance in the Quran's own divine-name list. | terra: Al-Muʾmin (ٱلْمُؤْمِنُ) appears as a divine name, directly supplying the section’s named sense of God as guarantor of His word.

luna: The section explicitly says lying is said of both speech and action; this address asks believers why they say what they do not do, naming the same gap between words and deeds. | terra: Believers are asked why they say what they do not do, making the truth-value of speech answerable to action.

luna: This continuation says God greatly detests saying what one does not do; it supplies the judgment on the speech/action mismatch named in 61:2 and in the section's dictionary note. | terra: God greatly hates saying what one does not do; this gives the moral verdict on the word-and-deed fracture named in 61:2.

luna: The section says trust depends on truthful speech and a reliable speaker; the hypocrites testify that Muhammad is God's Messenger, but God calls them liars, separating a true sentence from the speaker's false stance. | terra: The hypocrites utter a proposition that is factually true, yet God witnesses that they are liars; their stance makes their speech false despite its surface.

luna: The section says a lie can be an act as well as a statement; these speakers use their oaths as a shield and turn people from God's way, giving their false testimony a deceptive function. | terra: The hypocrites use their oaths as a shield and obstruct God’s way; this ayah supplies the action performed by the false testimony exposed in 63:1.

luna: The section's dictionary example of a lying cloth concerns an attractive surface that misrepresents its reality; this verse says the hypocrites' bodies impress and their speech draws listeners, yet compares them to propped-up timber, a specific outward/inward mismatch. | terra: Their bodies impress and their speech attracts hearing, yet they are likened to propped timber; outward pattern and inward reality diverge like the section’s deceptive fabric.
luna: God created the heavens and earth in truth, formed people, and made their forms beautiful; the verse then says they return to Him, joining the section's creation and judgment sequence.
terra: Those who disbelieve claim they will not be raised; the Prophet must answer “Yes, by my Lord,” followed by certain informing and recompense.
terra: Whoever believes in God has the heart guided by Him, directly joining īmān to the heart’s right placement under affliction.

luna: The section asks which making is real and which is fabricated; here God sets an absolute boundary, saying that if the Messenger had fabricated words against Him, He would seize him, so revelation cannot be treated as a human invention. | terra: The possibility that the Messenger might fabricate sayings in God’s name is raised only to declare the consequence that would follow, sharply guarding the trustworthiness of transmitted revelation.
luna: The continuation says God would cut the Messenger's aorta if he fabricated words; it completes the boundary stated in 69:44 with the stated consequence.
luna: The next verse says none of them could prevent that consequence; it closes the passage's proof that the Messenger does not invent speech about God.
terra: Those who affirm the Day of Judgment (يُصَدِّقُونَ بِيَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ) are the direct positive reversal of those who deny it.

luna: This repeated formulation says believers preserve their trusts and pledges; it concretely echoes the section's amānah/emīn link and binds reliability to their other acts of worship. | terra: Guarding trusts and covenants recurs among the qualities of those stable in prayer, again making trustworthiness a practiced state.
terra: The promised Day rends the sky, and God’s promise is described as accomplished; the judgment denied now becomes a completed event.

luna: The section quotes the people of Hell saying وَكُنَّا نُكَذِّبُ بِيَوْمِ الدِّينِ; here they confess that denying the Day of Judgment was among the reasons they entered Saqar. | terra: The people of the Fire confess that they used to deny the Day of Judgment, turning present denial into retrospective self-testimony.
luna: The next confession says they persisted until certainty came; it completes the admission in 74:46 by naming what ended their period of denial.
terra: The denier “neither confirmed nor prayed”; this negative prepares 75:32’s positive act of denial and contrasts with faith as tasdīq.
terra: “He denied and turned away” makes rejection both a judgment about truth and an enacted withdrawal.
luna: The section asks how people can deny the dīn after being created; this passage asks whether a human thinks he will be left without purpose or accountability.
luna: The next verse recalls the human's beginning as a drop of semen; it provides the created origin behind the question about being left unaccountable.
luna: The next step is that God made the drop into a clot, then created and proportioned it; this is a specific creation sequence that answers the section's claim about the human's made form.
luna: The continuation says God made from it the two sexes, completing the account of bodily creation that leads to the question about resurrection.

luna: The passage concludes by asking whether the One who did this can revive the dead; like the section's challenge after human creation, it connects making with the coming judgment. | terra: After rehearsing the human’s creation, “Is He not able to revive the dead?” uses the same fixed-answer form as 95:8 to answer denial of return.
luna: The section cites the carrier as obedient and trustworthy in 81:21; this passage first identifies the message as brought by a noble messenger, establishing who bears it.
luna: The continuation describes that messenger as powerful and established near the Lord of the Throne; it gives the standing of the carrier called trustworthy in 81:21.

luna: The section directly cites مُطَاعٍ ثَمَّ أَمِينٍ: the messenger is obeyed there and trustworthy, a precise description of faithful transmission. | terra: The revelatory messenger is obeyed and trustworthy, confirming the reliability of the transmission before human acceptance or denial.
luna: This verse says the messenger is not withholding the unseen; it adds a specific mark of disclosure to the trustworthiness stated in 81:21.
luna: The section cites the trustworthy carrier of revelation; this verse says the Quran is not the word of an expelled devil, a specific boundary against false attribution.
terra: “What has deceived you concerning your generous Lord?” opens a sequence that recalls creation in 82:7 and identifies denial of judgment in 82:9.

luna: The section's root gloss for خ ل ق contrasts true making with fabricated claims; this verse says God خلق the human and fashioned him, grounding 95:4's human creation in an explicit account of proportioning. | terra: God created, proportioned, and balanced the human being; this creation is the evidence immediately preceding 82:9’s denial of Judgment, closely paralleling 95:4–7.
luna: The section's 95:4 image is a human made in excellent form; this next verse says God assembled the person in whatever صورة He willed, giving the concrete bodily form that 82:7 introduces.

luna: The section asks how anyone can deny the dīn after God made the human; this immediate continuation says بل تكذبون بالدين, placing denial of recompense directly after the creation and fashioning in 82:7–8. | terra: “Rather, you deny the Judgment” (تُكَذِّبُونَ بِٱلدِّينِ) is the closest independent formulation of the denial named in 95:7.
luna: The section cites the deniers of the Day of Judgment among people who cheat in measure; this opening woe introduces those traders, whose conduct 83:11 explicitly links to denying that Day.
luna: The trader demands a full measure when taking for himself; this is one side of the specific cheating scene that the section connects to denial of judgment.
luna: When measuring or weighing for others, the trader gives less; this completes the asymmetry in the fraud scene before 83:11 names denial of the Day.

luna: The section explicitly cites الَّذِينَ يُكَذِّبُونَ بِيَوْمِ الدِّينِ about those who cheat in measure; this verse names their denial of the Day of Judgment. | terra: The transgressors are identified as those who deny the Day of Judgment, giving the object of the denial its eschatological setting.

luna: On the Day of judgment, the deniers are told “this is what you used to deny”; it completes the contrast between their earlier denial in 83:11 and the judgment they face. | terra: On the Day itself they are told, “This is what you used to deny”; the cited ayah supplies the encounter with what 83:11 says they rejected.
terra: The human is commanded to consider from what he was created, beginning an evidentiary sequence that concludes with God’s power to return him in 86:8.
terra: After naming the human’s created origin, the passage states that God is able to return him, making first creation evidence for the contested return.

luna: The address to the tranquil soul (النَّفْسُ الْمُطْمَئِنَّةُ) directly echoes the section's dictionary account of security as calmness and fear gone. | terra: The “reassured soul” is called to return to its Lord pleased and pleasing, showing settledness at the point when the divine promise is fulfilled.
luna: The tranquil soul is told to return to its Lord, pleased and pleasing; this joins the section's calm heart with its ر د د theme of return and its promise of reward.
luna: The next verse welcomes the soul among God's servants; it develops the secure return of 89:28 into belonging among the faithful.
luna: The final command is to enter Paradise; it completes the welcome and lasting reward that stand opposite the denial of dīn in the section.
luna: This oath opens with “this city” (بِهَٰذَا الْبَلَدِ), the same city wording as 95:3; it places the surah's secure city inside a wider Quranic address to the city itself.
luna: The next oath says the Prophet is dwelling in this city; it adds the Messenger's presence to the city's scene named in 90:1, alongside 95:3's “secure city.”
terra: Confirming “the best” is the accepting response that leads toward ease, providing the positive side of the trust/denial divide.
terra: Denying “the best” reverses 92:6 and leads toward hardship, so acceptance and rejection disclose their practical directions.
terra: The Prophet is reminded that God expanded his breast, a bodily image of the inward capaciousness named under the root of balad.

luna: The section explicitly cites the question about one who كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ, denies and turns away; this verse gives that paired action as the challenge to the one preventing prayer. | terra: The question “What if he denies and turns away?” immediately after surah 95 pairs false judgment of the message with conduct that enacts the rejection.
luna: The next verse asks whether he does not know that God sees; it completes the denial-and-turning-away scene with the awareness of divine witness.
luna: People whose scales are heavy are placed in a pleasing life; this makes the scale of deeds a concrete image of the judgment that measure-fraud deniers reject.
luna: The next verse names the heavy-scale outcome as a pleasing life, giving the reward side of the judgment introduced in 101:6.
luna: The opposite case is one whose scales are light, a direct reversal of the fair accounting that dishonest traders deny.
luna: The verse names the light-scale person's destination as the Abyss, completing the negative outcome of 101:8.
luna: The next verse asks what the Abyss is, extending the judgment scene rather than leaving the consequence unnamed.
luna: The final verse answers that the Abyss is a blazing fire, completing the fate attached to the light scales.

luna: God is said to have fed the Quraysh against hunger and made them safe from fear (وَآمَنَهُم مِّنْ خَوْفٍ); it states the fear-removing sense that the section gives to ء م ن. | terra: God “made them safe from fear” (ءَامَنَهُم مِّنْ خَوْفٍ), almost glossing the section’s definition of security as fear’s removal.

luna: The section explicitly cites أَرَأَيْتَ الَّذِي يُكَذِّبُ بِالدِّينِ; this verse asks the reader to look at the one who denies the dīn, the very denial the section puts opposite trust and belief. | terra: The Prophet is asked to look at the person who “denies the Judgment,” restaging 95:7 as an observable human type.
luna: The next verse identifies the denier by his act of repelling the orphan, showing how denial of the dīn appears in treatment of another person.
luna: The continuation adds that he does not urge feeding the poor; it completes the practical description of the denier begun in 107:1–2.
